column1: # title|accuracy rationale|substance rationale|language rationale|themes|Scripture references|wording to examine|concern|new text scores (accuracy,substance,language)

May the Mind of Christ My Savior|The prayer seeks Christ's character, God's word and the Father's peace to govern ordinary conduct; victory is attributed to divine power rather than independent moral improvement.|The successive petitions develop thought, speech, comfort of sufferers, self-forgetting love, perseverance and witness. Inner formation is consistently directed toward outward service.|Each stanza adds a distinct petition within a clear shared pattern. The closing channel image asks witnesses to point beyond themselves, rather than treating the Christian worker as the source of saving power.|Sanctification;Scripture;Humility;Witness|Philippians 2:5;Colossians 3:16;Hebrews 12:2|||9,8,9

Man of Sorrows! What a Name|The sinless Son takes the condemned sinner's place and seals pardon with his blood; the closing stanzas add exaltation and return. Salvation is not reduced to admiration of suffering.|Incarnation, human guilt, substitution, completed atonement, heavenly reign and final gathering give the short stanzas substantial gospel content.|The recurring exclamation answers a new saving claim each time. Older vocabulary about scoffing and the ransom should be explained, while the contrast between guilty sinners and the spotless Lamb remains clear.|Atonement;Forgiveness;Reign of Christ;Return of Christ|Isaiah 53:3;2 Corinthians 5:21;John 19:30|||10,9,9

Up from the Grave He Arose|Jesus' resurrection is presented as real victory over death and the grave, followed by enduring life and reign with his people. Human guards and seals cannot prevent divine victory.|Burial, failed attempts to secure the tomb, death's defeat and lasting reign give the refrain several supports. The text focuses on resurrection rather than explaining the cross's saving mechanism.|The contrast between quiet burial verses and triumphant refrain is inherent in the words. Describing death as a defeated captor is recognizable personification rather than a separate account of events beneath the grave.|Resurrection;Victory over death;Reign of Christ|Matthew 28:6;Acts 2:24;Romans 6:9|||9,7,8

Dying with Jesus (Moment by Moment)|The text grounds continuing life and preservation in union with Jesus, then describes his presence within trial rather than an escape from every burden.|Dependence is applied to sorrow, weakness, danger, sickness and ordinary time. The recurring assurance is supported by several concrete forms of need rather than left undefined.|The repeated moment refrain expresses ongoing reliance coherently. The statement about Christ's ability to heal concerns his power, not a promise that all sickness will be removed immediately.|Union with Christ;Dependence;Preservation|Galatians 2:20;John 15:5;Hebrews 4:15|||9,7,8

O Church Arise|The church's strength is supplied by God, and its warfare explicitly loves captive people while resisting the devil's lies. The cross and resurrection ground the secure outcome rather than the church's aggression.|Spiritual armor, loving mission, atonement, resurrection, dependence on the Spirit and final perseverance build a broad account of Christian service.|The martial image is bounded by truth, faith and love rather than literal violence. The closing race and witness imagery extends the call toward faithful endurance.|Church;Spiritual warfare;Mission;Perseverance|Ephesians 6:13;Ephesians 6:17;Hebrews 12:1|||9,9,8

By Faith|Faith responds to God's promise, Christ's victory and the Spirit's mission rather than creating reality by human certainty. The closing possibilities must remain governed by that gospel setting.|The text traces creation, the patriarchs' hope, prophetic expectation, resurrection and the church's worldwide calling. Endurance is directed toward God himself as reward.|The recurring faith pattern gives historical movement a clear structure. The mountain image needs contextual teaching so it does not become an unrestricted promise that all chosen outcomes follow sufficient confidence.|Faith;Promise;Resurrection;Mission|Hebrews 11:10;Hebrews 12:2;2 Corinthians 5:7|By faith, this mountain shall be moved|Read the image within the surrounding claim that the gospel prevails through Christ. It is not a guarantee that every hardship or personal obstacle disappears when a believer has enough faith.|8,8,8

Across the Lands|The eternal Word creates and sustains all things, enters human life, suffers so the guilty go free and rises to intercede. Christ's deity, humanity and saving work are held together.|Creation, incarnation, earthly ministry, atonement, resurrection, ascension, intercession and worldwide gathering form an unusually broad narrative.|The repeated royal confession unifies the narrative. Speech, silence at suffering and victorious proclamation form a coherent poetic sequence; the resurrection shout is a poetic scene rather than an explicit Gospel quotation.|Creation;Incarnation;Atonement;Intercession|Colossians 1:16;John 1:14;Hebrews 7:25|||9,9,9

There Is a Higher Throne|People from every tongue stand faultless through the Lamb and receive promised grace; belonging before God's throne is not earned by the perfection of their present singing.|Heavenly worship, gracious acceptance, the end of grief and the Lamb's shepherding rule develop the hope beyond earthly authority. The final home has both personal comfort and corporate worship.|Jewelled heavenly imagery draws on Revelation and may need explanation. The movement from distant throne to shared home makes the vision more than decorative description.|Eternal hope;Grace;Heavenly worship;Reign of Christ|Revelation 7:9;Revelation 7:17;Revelation 21:4|||9,8,8

Come Behold the Wondrous Mystery|The sinless incarnate Son fulfills the law and dies in sinners' place, then rises as the ground of their future resurrection. Mystery does not mean the central saving claims are withheld.|Incarnation, Christ as the better Adam, substitution, the Father's saving purpose and resurrection hope develop in successive stanzas. The promised deliverance is grounded in Christ's own victory.|The recurring invitation introduces a new stage rather than replacing exposition. The apparent paradox of the God of life undergoing death should be read through Christ's genuine humanity without denying his deity.|Incarnation;Atonement;Resurrection;Eternal hope|Romans 5:19;1 Peter 2:24;1 Corinthians 15:20|||10,9,9

My Worth Is Not in What I Own|Worth and acceptance are located in Christ's costly ransom rather than possessions, achievement, physical strength or human wisdom. Confessing unworthiness guards against turning personal value into a claim of moral deserving.|The verses address status, success and failure, mortality, misplaced boasting and costly redemption; the refrain turns from those false securities to satisfaction in Christ.|The repeated rejection of inadequate grounds builds a coherent argument. Holding value and unworthiness together is an intentional distinction between being graciously loved and deserving redemption.|Grace;Atonement;Humility;Satisfaction in Christ|Galatians 6:14;1 Peter 1:18;Philippians 3:8|||9,8,9

The Lord Is My Salvation|Grace initiates rescue, the debt is paid and resurrection completes the hope; the final praise explicitly names Father, Son and Spirit. Confidence rests on God's saving work rather than optimism.|Rescue, fear, promise, waiting, loss, weakness, death and Trinitarian praise develop salvation across the believer's life. The verses acknowledge difficult seasons instead of excluding them.|The repeated salvation claim receives concrete support in each verse. Seasonal imagery points to hope and renewal, while the resurrection stanza prevents it from becoming merely a promise of improved circumstances.|Salvation;Grace;Perseverance;Trinity|Psalm 27:1;Romans 8:11;Titus 3:5|||9,8,8

Lord, from Sorrows Deep I Call|The prayer directs a shaken soul to God as salvation while openly acknowledging unanswered prayer and a remaining thorn. Praise is not presented as a transaction that guarantees suffering ends.|Lament, unanswered questions, loss of earthly goods, divine refuge and future sight give the song pastoral and theological development. The singer asks God to sustain praise amid grief.|The alternation between addressing God and addressing the soul follows the pattern of biblical lament. The storm image supports honest endurance rather than denying continuing pain.|Lament;Trust;Refuge;Perseverance|Psalm 42:5;2 Corinthians 12:9;Habakkuk 3:18|||9,8,9

Christ the Sure and Steady Anchor|Assurance is fixed in Christ's steadfastness and the love proved at Calvary rather than in the absence of doubt or accusation. The final hope passes through death to secured life.|Suffering, temptation, guilt, unbelief, the cross and death develop the anchor metaphor through successive trials. Clinging is a response to Christ's reliability rather than an independent saving achievement.|The extended nautical image is sustained with storms, ballast, horizon and shore. Its shifts serve the same promise of security, while continuing storms prevent a reading of instant earthly relief.|Assurance;Atonement;Perseverance;Eternal hope|Hebrews 6:19;Romans 5:8;Hebrews 12:2|||9,8,9

Ancient of Days (Blessing and Honor)|The selected Sadler/Harvill text confesses eternal divine kingship and universal worship rather than exalting a present human ruler. Nations and creation are summoned to acknowledge God's glory.|The enduring kingdom, unmatched worth and worship of the nations supply successive grounds for praise, while the saving work of Christ is less developed.|The ancient throne title and corporate invitation form a coherent biblical setting. This acclamation beginning with blessing and honor is a different text from CityAlight's song sharing the shorter title.|Kingship;Eternity;Corporate praise|Daniel 7:9;Daniel 7:14;Revelation 5:13|||9,7,8

O Great God|God's prior love and purchase ground the request for holiness, while the Spirit gives life through the Son's gospel. Obedience is sought through continuing dependence on grace rather than self-salvation.|The three verses develop repentance, regeneration through word and Spirit, and practical sanctification. The final goal includes thought and deed, not only a moment of worshipful feeling.|The royal and conflict images concern sin within the singer's heart, making the petition concrete without directing hostility at other people. The progression from blindness to life and dependent conduct is clear.|Sanctification;Regeneration;Grace;Holy Spirit|Titus 3:5;2 Corinthians 4:6;Romans 12:1|||9,9,8

Jesus, Thank You|The cross is presented as substitution, cleansing and satisfied judgment that reconciles former enemies to God. The perfect sacrifice grounds friendship and access rather than the singer's grateful performance.|Atonement, wrath, reconciliation, grace and responsive devotion develop a substantial gospel argument. Mystery acknowledges wonder without leaving the saving claims unspecified.|The table image makes reconciliation concrete and the recurring thanks has explained grounds. The verse addresses the Father while the chorus addresses Jesus, a change of addressee that should remain clear.|Atonement;Reconciliation;Gratitude;Grace|Romans 5:10;1 Peter 2:24;Ephesians 2:13|||9,9,8

Turn Your Eyes|The added verses identify the Son's death as erasing debt and join resurrection with the King's return. The invitation to look to Christ therefore has a defined gospel object rather than mere spiritual concentration.|Cross, resurrection, present devotion and final universal acknowledgment provide a broad narrative. The inherited earthly-dimming image concerns reordered affection rather than neglect of earthly responsibilities.|Each new scene gives the recurring invitation more content. A biological image of shared life requires explanation so that union with Christ is not confused with literal divine material in believers.|Devotion;Atonement;Resurrection;Return of Christ|Colossians 3:1;Colossians 2:14;Philippians 2:10|we carry His life in our veins|Read this as poetic participation in Christ's risen life by the Spirit, not literal divine blood or a guarantee of bodily immunity. Apply the same care to this image as to similar vein language in other songs.|8,8,8

Show Us Christ|The prayer seeks revelation of Christ through the preached word and asks God to overcome unbelief. It locates transformation in divine truth rather than a spectacle or a technique controlled by the congregation.|Receiving Scripture, fruitful obedience, wisdom, resistance to temptation and confession of Christ's lordship develop the petition. The word's life-giving function is illustrated in several distinct ways.|Seed, light and food images share a clear subject: God's word received by needy hearers. The final question reinforces dependence on the Lord's words rather than introducing a disconnected refrain.|Scripture;Prayer;Sanctification;Christ's lordship|Luke 8:15;Psalm 119:105;John 6:68|||9,8,8

Let Your Kingdom Come|Mission is a response to the cross that saved the singers and depends on God's strength and grace. The prayer seeks God's renown rather than the congregation's power, status or personal gain.|The first verse identifies the mission's object, the chorus its worldwide reach and the second verse the courage and perseverance required. Weak human agents remain dependent on God.|The kingdom petition receives concrete content in making Christ known and preaching the gospel. Its broad language should therefore be read within that stated mission rather than as a mandate for a preferred political program.|Mission;Kingdom of God;Grace;Perseverance|Matthew 6:10;Matthew 28:19;2 Corinthians 4:7|||9,8,8

The Glories of Calvary|Christ's costly death is said to conquer sin and remove holy wrath, while the risen Lamb receives praise. Redemption rests on his wounds rather than the intensity of the singer's response.|Grace, sin, mercy, reconciliation, resurrection and united earthly/heavenly praise give the recurring cross theme several developed dimensions.|The invitation to explore and the request to go deeper lead to specific saving claims, avoiding an undefined appeal for heightened emotion. The expansive song-count image is transparent poetic abundance.|Atonement;Grace;Forgiveness;Praise of Christ|Romans 5:9;1 Peter 2:24;Revelation 5:12|||9,8,8

Come Praise and Glorify|The Father adopts through the Son, redemption is received through Christ's sacrifice and the Spirit seals believers' hope. The final Trinitarian confession follows the work of the three persons rather than merely naming them.|Adoption, redemption, God's revealed purpose and the Spirit's guarantee form a sustained account of Ephesians 1. Praise is repeatedly tied to mercy and grace instead of human deserving.|The three-stanza structure and shared refrain keep a dense text coherent. Predestination language closely follows the passage but requires contextual teaching where traditions differ on its interpretation.|Trinity;Adoption;Redemption;Assurance|Ephesians 1:5;Ephesians 1:7;Ephesians 1:13|||9,9,8

Only a Holy God|God's holiness is joined with sovereign power, justice and fatherly rescue through the gift of his Son; holiness is not reduced to frightening distance or human moral achievement.|The verses supply distinct grounds for worship in creation's obedience, incomparable beauty, resurrection power and redemption. The final invitation to call God Father gives the praise a saving context.|Repeated questions make the argument easy to follow, and each returns to the same divine character. The movement from majesty to personal adoption gives the recurring invitation development.|Holiness;Sovereignty;Redemption;Adoption|Isaiah 6:3;John 3:16;Romans 8:15|||9,8,9

Good and Gracious King|Acceptance is received empty-handed on God's promise and love rather than purchased by the worshiper's offering; dependence on the Spirit and acknowledgment of divine self-sufficiency reinforce that grace.|The text develops approach to God, burden-bearing, joy in acceptance and secure belonging as a child and friend. It is less explicit about the cross that grounds access to the throne.|The repeated empty-hand image connects the verses and refrain, keeping praise a grateful response rather than a transaction. Royal and family language are understandable and complementary.|Grace;Acceptance;Prayer;Adoption|Hebrews 4:16;Ephesians 2:8;Acts 17:25|||9,7,8

Jesus, Strong and Kind|The verses invite thirsty, weak and fearful people to Jesus, and the final verse anchors his seeking love at the cross. Dependence is directed to Christ rather than the singer's resolve.|Several forms of need receive a specific response: satisfaction, strength, protection and rescue. The cross adds a saving basis to the recurring assurance, though the song remains deliberately simple.|The short repeated pattern is clear for children and adults. References to what Jesus said summarize biblical invitations rather than purporting to reproduce one continuous saying verbatim.|Trust;Christ's kindness;Cross;Dependence|John 7:37;Matthew 11:28;Luke 19:10|||9,7,9

Saved My Soul|The text expressly attributes salvation to grace alone and says the King paid for sin; freedom is received from God rather than achieved by escaping independently.|Captivity and rescue, hope, atonement, enduring belonging and passage from death to life give the refrain several supports. Spiritual warfare remains subordinate to salvation by grace.|The past-captivity and present-life contrasts make the testimony clear. Grave imagery is best understood through spiritual regeneration rather than as a claim of a personal physical resurrection.|Salvation;Grace;Atonement;New life|Ephesians 2:5;Ephesians 2:8;Colossians 1:13|||9,7,8

Christ Is Mine Forevermore|The song confesses real sin and relies on Christ's payment for failure; it also expects suffering and hostility in union with Christ rather than promising that redemption prevents hardship.|Repentance, assurance, sorrow, sanctification, pilgrimage, spiritual armor and final fellowship form a substantial account of Christian life. Future hope gives a horizon to unresolved present darkness.|The recurring contrast between what is presently mine and what is eternally mine gives the song progression. Honest acknowledgement of pain prevents the final celebration from sounding like denial.|Assurance;Atonement;Suffering;Eternal hope|Romans 8:17;Philippians 1:6;1 Peter 1:4|||9,9,9

On That Day|Hope beyond death is explicitly grounded in Christ's resurrection and reign. Grief remains acknowledged, while final bodily rising and fellowship with the Savior supply the promised outcome.|Resurrection, present endurance, heavenly worship and completed joy develop the final-day theme. Christ's death for sin receives less exposition than resurrection and future hope.|Present weariness and future sight give the refrain a clear contrast. The closing father image expresses welcome, while the distinction between Father and Son should remain clear in teaching.|Resurrection;Return of Christ;Eternal life;Hope|1 Corinthians 15:20;1 Thessalonians 4:13;1 John 3:2|||9,7,8

There Is One Gospel|The Father plans salvation, the Son rescues through the cross and resurrection, and the Spirit leads the united church. Human boasting is expressly excluded rather than smuggled into gospel confidence.|The four verses develop gospel foundation, justice and mercy at the cross, resurrection hope and the church's shared pilgrimage. Each return to the central claim adds substantive support.|A repeated opening and closing frame a coherent narrative without making repetition the whole content. The movement from individual confidence to corporate unity broadens the congregation's response.|Gospel;Atonement;Resurrection;Church|1 Corinthians 15:3;Ephesians 2:8;Ephesians 4:4|||10,9,9

Grace|Righteousness and restored access to Christ are attributed to blood rather than merit; the unstained Prince of life takes the sinner's place. Grace is thus connected with costly redemption rather than lenience toward sin.|The verses develop rescue from death, worldwide invitation, substitution, restoration and preservation to the final home. The concise refrain names the benefit while the verses explain its basis.|Parallel statements about grace create unity, and the contrast between the sinless one and the sinner makes the central argument concrete. The mystery language acknowledges limits without replacing the saving claims.|Grace;Atonement;Restoration;Perseverance|Ephesians 2:8;2 Corinthians 5:21;Titus 3:5|||9,8,8

God Is for Us|The Father's gift of his Son grounds confidence that his love will not forsake believers. The valley and battle settings keep assurance from depending on easy circumstances or human strength.|Refuge, persevering love after stumbling, grace and victory over final separation develop the Romans 8 theme. The song's strongest promises concern God's keeping love rather than ordinary success.|The fortress metaphor gives protection a clear object, and the bridge explains the confidence behind the repeated question. The rhetoric should be heard as assurance in Christ rather than divine endorsement of every human conflict.|Assurance;Fatherly love;Perseverance;Grace|Romans 8:31;Romans 8:32;Romans 8:39|||9,8,8

It Was Finished Upon That Cross|Christ's completed saving work breaks the curse, grants full pardon and clothes the believer in his righteousness. Resurrection is included, so finished work does not erase the continuing significance of the risen Savior.|The text develops victory over evil, payment, justification, access to the Father, freedom from death and future glory. Several distinct benefits are tied to the cross rather than asserted without foundation.|The recurring completed-work claim gives coherence to the advancing verses. Death's defeat is intentionally expressed as triumphant poetry while the movement toward eternal glory acknowledges future completion.|Atonement;Justification;Resurrection;Eternal hope|John 19:30;Galatians 3:13;Romans 5:1|||10,9,9

Your Will Be Done|The prayer opposes self-exaltation and follows Christ's obedient acceptance of the cross; his sin-bearing and resurrection ground hope rather than the singer's ability to imitate him perfectly.|Personal submission, Gethsemane, atonement, perseverance, resurrection and the church's mission form a developed pattern of prayer. The final corporate petition moves beyond private comfort.|The recurring submission unifies changing personal and corporate settings. Jesus' garden prayer functions as a model without making the congregation's obedience equal to his unique saving burden.|Submission;Prayer;Atonement;Mission|Matthew 6:10;Luke 22:42;Philippians 2:8|||9,9,8

I Will Trust My Saviour Jesus|Trust rests on the Savior's completed gift and death for the singer, not simply on determination to feel confident. Weakness and doubt are brought to Christ rather than presented as barriers he cannot overcome.|The verses move through doubt, weakness, guidance and lifelong pilgrimage; the bridge supplies the cross as the reason for surrendering every part of life. Future rest gives endurance a clear destination.|The repeated promise to trust is balanced by a prayer for help to trust, preventing a purely self-reliant tone. The final journey image clarifies that faith persists through time.|Trust;Atonement;Perseverance;Guidance|Mark 9:24;Hebrews 12:2;Hebrews 13:5|||9,8,8

Known and Loved|Being known by God includes weakness and sin, yet assurance is anchored in Jesus' finished work and payment of debt. Acceptance is not founded on concealing failure or assembling a perfected self.|Creation, providential knowledge, honest dependence, atonement and future face-to-face fellowship develop the relationship theme. Personal comfort receives an explicit gospel basis.|The contrast between hiding and coming into Christ's light makes the response concrete. The closing unseen-path image extends the same dependence into future uncertainty.|Providence;Grace;Assurance;Atonement|Psalm 139:16;Colossians 2:14;1 Corinthians 13:12|||9,8,8

All My Ways Are Known to You|Confidence rests on God's knowledge and providence through poverty, loss and darkness; the song does not require favorable circumstances as evidence of divine care. Death is approached as passage to life with him.|Contrasting seasons of peace and trial, assurance of guidance and final hope develop the theme, though Christ's saving work is not explicitly explained in this text.|The repeated knowledge refrain connects each contrast and the final prayer asks for understanding rather than omniscient certainty. Providential language should not be used to call human evil morally good.|Providence;Trust;Guidance;Eternal hope|Psalm 139:3;Romans 8:28;Psalm 23:4|||8,7,8

The Night Song|God's unsleeping care and Jesus' rescue from darkness support rest, and resurrection supplies an enduring hope. One protection statement needs to be read in that final-security context rather than as a denial of earthly danger.|The text moves from God's watchfulness to honest fear, gratitude and resurrection. It is a simple bedtime confession rather than an extended account of redemption.|Night and shadow images make the setting concrete for children. The absolute protection phrase is readily misunderstood if it is taught without the distinction between final keeping and immediate physical safety.|Providence;Rest;Trust;Resurrection|Psalm 121:4;John 10:28;John 16:33|In the shadows none can harm me|Read this as confidence in God's ultimate keeping, not a guarantee that a child or adult cannot be injured during the night. Believers still face real harm and need ordinary protection and care.|8,6,8

The Love of the Father|The text holds together the risen Savior, the coming Spirit and the Father's love; belonging is purchased at a cost rather than asserted as a natural human entitlement.|Heavenly praise, resurrection, transfer from darkness, costly redemption and final home give the shared family confession several supports. The precise nature of that saving cost is brief rather than fully explained.|The invitation to join earthly and heavenly voices gives the corporate refrain a clear setting. The progression from redeemed life to final united praise creates a coherent direction.|Fatherly love;Redemption;Resurrection;Church|1 John 3:1;Colossians 1:13;1 Peter 1:18|||9,7,8

Jesus Is Alive|Hope is based on Jesus' bodily resurrection and victorious kingship, with freedom from condemnation named as its saving benefit. This does not mean believers never experience doubt or temptation after conversion.|The empty tomb, invitation to the needy, deliverance from shame and final defeat of death give multiple reasons for celebration. Atonement itself is less developed than resurrection victory.|Darkness and rising praise connect the setting and response. The sweeping freedom language should express a changed status and hope rather than suppress honest admission of present struggles.|Resurrection;Hope;Freedom;Assurance|1 Corinthians 15:20;Romans 8:1;John 16:33|No more doubt and fear|Treat this as triumphant confidence in Christ's victory, not a claim that genuine Christians cannot struggle with doubt or anxiety. The invitation to the worn and weak should remain open to those who still feel afraid.|8,7,8

This Is the Day|God's goodness is confessed in pain and death as well as favorable weather and joy; redemption and belonging ground rejoicing rather than a requirement to feel cheerful in every circumstance.|Creation's daily gift, providential guidance, salvation, God's reign and the future home develop the Psalm refrain. The song is broader than a generic celebration of a pleasant day.|The paired contrasts make the repeated call to rejoice intelligible during hardship. The bridge moves from today's praise to final hope, giving the refrain a direction beyond the present moment.|Praise;Providence;Salvation;Eternal hope|Psalm 118:24;1 Thessalonians 5:18;Romans 8:28|||9,7,8

My God Is All I Need|Dependence on God is confessed through darkness, tempting treasure and approaching death; rescue and the Savior give sufficiency a personal saving context. Divine power is praised rather than attributed to the singer.|Strength, peace, hope, liberation and mortality develop the main confession. The appended children's chorus adds creation and omnipotence, though it does not further explain redemption.|Short contrasts and the recurring need refrain suit a shared confession. The source includes a medley, so the additional power statements must be checked against the actual chosen text and taught as power consistent with God's character.|Dependence;Providence;Salvation;God's power|Psalm 73:25;2 Corinthians 12:9;Jeremiah 32:17|||9,7,8

catalog-ancient-of-days|The CityAlight text confesses God's enduring rule over changing nations and his personal presence amid fear; final hope is directed to the coming Savior King.|Political upheaval, inward dread and uncertainty about the future receive distinct answers in God's sovereignty, knowing love and final presence. The cross is not explicitly developed.|The recurring ancient-king title coheres with Daniel's throne vision. This is the CityAlight text beginning with raging nations, distinct from the Sadler/Harvill acclamation sharing its title.|Sovereignty;Assurance;Return of Christ|Daniel 7:9;Psalm 46:6;Revelation 22:4|||9,7,8

artist-ancient-of-days-shane-shane-the-worship-initiative|The selected CityAlight text confesses God's enduring rule over changing nations and his personal presence amid fear; hope culminates in the Savior King's coming.|National upheaval, inward dread and an unknown future each receive a developed answer. This reading concerns the selected CityAlight text and does not verify every word of the associated Shane & Shane recording.|The repeated royal title unifies the verses and connects with Daniel's vision. Distinguish this text beginning with raging nations from the separate Sadler/Harvill song of the same title.|Sovereignty;Assurance;Return of Christ|Daniel 7:9;Psalm 46:6;Revelation 22:4|||9,7,8

No Longer Slaves|The central confession links freedom from fear with belonging to God's family, and the second verse names new birth. Its assurance should be understood as a Christian confession, not a claim that all people are automatically regenerate.|Fatherly protection, deliverance and adoption provide several supports for the refrain, but the means of reconciliation through Christ's death are less explicit than the family imagery.|The exodus scene makes deliverance vivid and the refrain is clear. One biological image requires explanation so that spiritual adoption is not confused with sharing God's nature.|Adoption;Freedom from fear;Deliverance;New birth|Romans 8:15;John 1:12;1 John 4:18|Your blood flows through my veins|Read this as poetic family belonging through new birth, not a literal transfer of divine substance or a claim that believers become gods. Christians can also experience fear while learning to live in their adoption.|8,6,7

It Is Well (Through It All)|Trust is directed to the Lord who commands creation, and the refrain seeks assurance amid disturbance. The mountain promise requires biblical context rather than a guarantee that each chosen obstacle will disappear.|The text develops faith under uncertainty and dependence on God's power, but does not include the older hymn's sustained treatment of sin-bearing and the cross. The shared refrain does not make these complete texts interchangeable.|The storm image unifies the song and the refrain is immediately intelligible. The movement from trust to assured removal of the singer's mountain can overstate what the lyric itself establishes.|Trust;Peace;God's power;Perseverance|Mark 4:39;Mark 11:23;John 16:33|will be thrown into the midst of the sea|The mountain image echoes Jesus' teaching about faith and prayer. It should not be taught as a guarantee that sincere believers can remove any hardship on demand or as a judgment on sufferers whose circumstances persist.|7,5,7

Washed|The verses expressly distinguish Christ's work from the singer's achievements and identify Calvary as the basis of redemption. Cleansing and victory are received gifts rather than a reward for performance.|Sin, shame, ransom, mercy and the cross give the celebration substantial gospel content. The water-and-blood pairing raises a baptismal question that requires more precision than the refrain supplies.|The washing and resurrection images make a coherent movement from guilt to restored life. The exuberant grave metaphor is spiritual participation in Christ's life, not a report that every singer has physically risen.|Atonement;Cleansing;Grace;New life|1 John 1:7;Titus 3:5;Colossians 2:13|washed in the water|The source pairs water with Christ's blood. Traditions differ on baptism's relationship to regeneration; explain that reading instead of treating the phrase as proof of either automatic sacramental salvation or a rejection of baptism.|8,7,8

Goodbye Yesterday|The text names new birth, the Spirit and following Jesus, and presents rescue as something God accomplishes. Its resurrection imagery should mean new life in Christ rather than a bodily or divine property in the singer's blood.|Turning from former ways, repeated rescue and costly discipleship provide several distinct themes. The saving death of Christ is suggested by the cross but not explained as fully as the new-life celebration.|The contrast of past captivity and present freedom is clear, and the borrowed discipleship refrain sharpens the response. The biological resurrection image is more ambiguous than the otherwise concrete language.|New birth;Conversion;Discipleship;New life|2 Corinthians 5:17;Romans 6:4;Luke 9:23|resurrection in my veins|Treat this as a metaphor for new life by the Spirit, not literal resurrection material or a promise of bodily invulnerability. The lyric does not establish a doctrine of divine substance within believers.|8,6,7

At the Altar|The second verse explicitly attributes cleansing and freedom to grace for a sinner; surrender is therefore a response to rescue rather than a payment that makes God accept the worshiper.|Repentant removal of hindrances, gratitude, costly devotion and entrusting grief to God develop the central offering image. The actual saving work behind that grace remains relatively compressed.|The altar image joins the verses and chorus, but a sweeping assurance about anxiety can sound like a guaranteed immediate emotional cure. Explain the difference between an invitation to entrust fear and a prediction about symptoms.|Surrender;Repentance;Grace;Devotion|Romans 12:1;Psalm 51:17;1 Peter 5:7|Fear and anxiety cannot live here|This can express the desired fruit of trusting God, but worship does not guarantee that anxiety instantly disappears. Avoid implying that persistent fear proves a person failed to surrender or cannot belong in worship.|7,6,7

Good Plans|Confidence is grounded in the Lord as shepherd and savior, and the explicit valley and desert settings acknowledge adversity. God's good purposes should not be equated with the singer's preferred outcomes.|The song develops provision, presence, protection and enduring mercy through Psalm 23's images. Its references to victory and weapons need the wider biblical account of faithful suffering.|The garden-and-desert contrast helps prevent an exclusively prosperous reading.
